## Motivation {.content-slide}

::::: columns
::: {.column width="53%"}
- Border closures can reshape access to markets, suppliers, and jobs.
- In border regions, the relevant shock is often not geography alone, but road-network access to an open crossing.
- The Colombia-Venezuela border is a strong case because formal access changed sharply after 2019.
- Nighttime lights give a quarterly proxy for local economic activity when standard statistics are sparse.
:::

::: {.column width="47%"}
![Al Jazeera, 9 Sep 2022](../presentation/assets/aljazeera.png){width="100%"}
:::
:::::

## Introduction {.content-slide}

::::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
### Research question

How did changes in road-network access to the Colombia-Venezuela border affect local economic activity?

### Contribution

- Continuous exposure measure based on network distance
- Quarterly municipality panel built from GIS and satellite data
- Border-specific evidence on how access shocks map into local outcomes
:::

::::: {.column width="48%"}
::: callout-tip
### What is new here?

I do not treat the border as a simple dummy. I measure how much the nearest usable crossing effectively moved after restrictions.
:::

::: callout-note
### Why that matters

Two municipalities can sit equally close to the border and still face very different access shocks once roads and crossings are taken seriously.
:::
:::::
:::::::

## Conceptual framework {.content-slide}

:::::: concept-grid
::: concept-card
**Policy shock** Border closures and reopenings change which crossings are usable.
:::

::: concept-card
**Transmission channel** Road-network detours raise travel cost and weaken cross-border interaction.
:::

::: concept-card
**Outcome** Lower accessibility should show up as weaker nighttime-light activity.
:::
::::::

::: callout-note
Expected sign: more access loss, lower activity.
:::

#### Existing literature

:::::: concept-grid
::: concept-card
**1. Border and trade costs** Anderson & van Wincoop (2003); Brülhart et al. (2012); Heiland et al. (2019)
:::

::: concept-card
**2. Transport infrastructure and access** Redding & Turner (2015); Donaldson (2018); Banerjee et al. (2020)
:::

::: concept-card
**3. Remote sensing and nighttime lights** Henderson et al. (2012); Pinkovskiy & Sala-i-Martin (2016); Beyer et al. (2022)
:::
::::::

## Methodology {.content-slide}

### Empirical pipeline - Implementation of Behrens (2024)

:::::::::::::::::: columns
:::::::::::::::: {.column width="100%"}
::::::::::::::: pipeline
::::: pipeline-step
::: step-number
1
:::

::: step-text
<strong>Build the road network</strong><br>Use the motorcar network to connect municipalities to the border system.
:::
:::::

::::: pipeline-step
::: step-number
2
:::

::: step-text
<strong>Define crossing regimesr</strong><br>Identify which formal crossings are operational before and after the 2019 disruption.
:::
:::::

::::: pipeline-step
::: step-number
3
:::

::: step-text
<strong>Measure access</strong><br>Compute shortest-path road-network distances and define treatment intensity as 
$D_i = \log(d_i^{post}) - \log(d_i^{pre})$

:::
:::::

::::: pipeline-step
::: step-number
4
:::

::: step-text
<strong>Construct exposure</strong><br>Interact $D_i$ with the municipality-quarter post indicator to build exposure intensity.
:::
:::::

::::: pipeline-step
::: step-number
5
:::

::: step-text
<strong>Estimate effects</strong><br>Run fixed-effects models and dynamic event-study checks.
:::
:::::
:::::::::::::::
::::::::::::::::

## Methodology {.content-slide}

### Baseline model and specifications

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
$$
Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \gamma_t + \beta \, Exposure_{it} + \varepsilon_{it}
$$

where:

- $Y_{it}$ = log(1 + nighttime lights) in municipality $i$ at time $t$
- $\alpha_i$ = municipality fixed effects, absorbing time-invariant local characteristics
- $\gamma_t$ = quarter fixed effects, absorbing common shocks across all municipalities
- $Exposure_{it}$ = its the treatment intensity interacted with the post period indicator.
- $\beta$ = effect of a one-unit increase in exposure on local economic activity
:::

:::: {.column width="48%"}

| Specification                 | Purpose                      |
|-------------------------------|------------------------------|
| TWFE                          | Baseline comparison          |
| Country x quarter FE          | Absorb national shocks       |
| Corridor x quarter FE         | Absorb border-system shocks  |
| State/department x quarter FE | Absorb local regional shocks |

::: callout-important
### Identification logic

If the estimated effect survives tighter local time controls, it is more likely to reflect access rather than broader regional shocks.
:::
::::
::::::

## Data {.content-slide}

:::::::: columns
::::: {.column width="60%"}
| Data | Source | Role |
|------------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Municipalities | Administrative boundaries | Panel units |
| Roads | OpenStreetMap motorcar network | Shortest-path access measures |
| Crossings | Georeferenced border crossings + institutional records | Access regime and closure dates |
| Outcome | VIIRS nighttime lights | Quarterly economic activity proxy |

::: callout-note
Baseline estimation window

- 2017Q1 to 2018Q4: clean pre-period
- 2019Q1: transition quarter, excluded
- 2019Q2 to 2022Q2: clean closure period
:::

## Results {.content-slide}

### Main estimates

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="54%"}
![Coefficient sensitivity](../Output/Figures/final/figure_main_coefficient_sensitivity.png){width="100%"}
:::

:::: {.column width="46%"}
### Main estimates

- Simple TWFE: -0.0168 (p = 0.033)
- Country x quarter FE: -0.0104 (p = 0.146)
- State/department x quarter FE: -0.0057 (p = 0.616)
- Municipality-specific trends: -0.00043 (p = 0.977)

::: callout-note
The negative coefficient shrinks quickly once tighter local controls are added.
:::
::::
::::::

## Results {.content-slide}

### Dynamic check

:::::: columns
::: {.column width="52%"}
![Event-study around the border disruption](../Output/Figures/final/figure_event_study_region_fe.png){width="100%"}
:::

:::: {.column width="48%"}
### Dynamic check

- Event-study estimates show differential pre-trends.
- The dynamic pattern weakens with more localized controls, but it does not disappear completely.
- Under the preferred state/department-by-quarter specification, the joint pre-treatment test gives an F-statistic of approximately 2.32 and a p-value of 0.027

::: callout-important
This is the main reason I avoid over-claiming a clean causal effect.
:::
::::
::::::

## Results {.content-slide}

### Reopening and heterogeneity

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
![Reopening validation](../Output/Figures/final/figure_reopening_event_study.png){width="100%"}
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![Country heterogeneity](../Output/Figures/final/figure_country_heterogeneity.png){width="100%"}
:::
:::::

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Reopening check

- Positive reopening coefficient
- Municipalities with larger past access losses recover more when access is restored
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Heterogeneity

- Colombia: positive and borderline significant
- Venezuela: negative but statistically imprecise
:::
:::::

## Conclusion {.content-slide}

::: callout-tip
### Bottom line

Border accessibility appears to matter, but the strongest evidence is supportive rather than definitive causal proof.
:::

- Larger access losses are associated with weaker local nighttime-light activity in border municipalities.
- The baseline effect is sensitive to tighter local time controls, so the causal claim should remain cautious.
- The reopening pattern is consistent with the proposed accessibility mechanism, but also warrants caution.
